5. My Thoughts, Criticisms & Unstated Limitations

Criticism 1 (AI): The Malignancy “Catch-22” (Label Requirement):

The framework’s method for determining if a shift is harmful requires passing the most anomalous target samples to an “external labeling function.” In real-world unsupervised deployment—where distribution shift detection is most critical precisely because we lack labels—this is a massive, often prohibitive assumption. While they argue you only need to label a tiny fraction of data, waiting for human-in-the-loop labeling defeats the purpose of an automated, real-time “loud failure.”

Criticism 2 (AI): Batch vs. Streaming Evaluation:

The methodology relies on classical two-sample testing (p vs q), which inherently assumes we are comparing two static batches of data. Real-world ML pipelines face continuous, time-correlated data streams. Standard KS or MMD tests assume i.i.d. samples within the target window; if the incoming stream has temporal auto-correlation, these tests will throw massive false-positive alarms. The authors briefly acknowledge this in their conclusion, but it remains a critical barrier to out-of-the-box deployment.

Criticism 3 (AI): Image-Centric Bias & Softmax Geometries:

The finding that BBSDs (Softmax outputs) is the ultimate DR technique is highly specific to the geometry of neural networks trained on image classification (ResNet-18). Does this hold up in tabular environments using Gradient Boosted Trees? Does it hold in LLMs? Softmax calibration degrades terribly under shift; while this makes it great for detecting that a shift occurred, it might be overly sensitive to entirely benign shifts in strictly bounded tabular domains.

Criticism 4 (AI): The Danger of the Bonferroni Correction:

Using multiple univariate KS tests combined with a Bonferroni correction worked well here because the latent dimension \(K\) was small (\(K=10\) for BBSDs on CIFAR/MNIST). However, Bonferroni scales terribly. If applied to an ImageNet classifier (\(K=1000\)), the threshold \(\alpha/K\) becomes so conservative that the statistical power of the test would likely vanish, rendering the model blind to subtle shifts.

6. Action Items & Integration into My Work

Adopt BBSDs as a Core Baseline: Any framework I build for monitoring ML models in production must benchmark against BBSDs + KS Test. It is computationally virtually free (since the model is already computing softmax anyway) and serves as the gold-standard baseline.
Address the Malignancy Gap: Position my own research as solving the exact limitation this paper introduces: How do we determine shift malignancy entirely unsupervised, without requiring an external labeling oracle? (e.g., via predictive variance, entropy tracking, or self-consistency metrics).
Incorporate the “Domain Classifier” concept for Explainability: Use their method of ranking anomalies via Domain Classifier confidence to explain what shifted in my own datasets, rather than just firing a binary alarm.

title: How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression
text:
2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

The Motivation (Why this paper matters)
As machine learning models increasingly produce probabilistic predictions rather than single point forecasts, it becomes essential to evaluate the quality of their uncertainty estimates. In regression problems, uncertainty is typically expressed through predictive distributions, prediction intervals, or confidence intervals. However, the authors argue that current evaluation practice is fundamentally flawed and may incorrectly rank uncertainty estimation methods.
Two dominant evaluation strategies are widely used:

Predictive density evaluation using test log-likelihood.
Interval evaluation using metrics such as Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP).

The paper demonstrates that both approaches are insufficient for assessing the correctness of uncertainty estimates.



Central Problem Identified
The authors argue that commonly used metrics evaluate aggregate predictive performance, not whether the estimated uncertainty is actually correct. As a result, a model may appear well-calibrated even if its uncertainty estimates behave incorrectly across different regions of the input space.
For example:

A model may produce intervals that are too narrow in some regions and too wide in others, yet still achieve correct average coverage.
Log-likelihood improvements may arise from better mean predictions rather than improved uncertainty estimation.

Thus, existing evaluation metrics fail to isolate the true quality of uncertainty estimates.



Key Novelty
The main contribution of the paper is not a new predictive model, but a new evaluation framework for uncertainty estimates in regression.
The authors propose a simulation-based evaluation strategy that measures pointwise coverage instead of relying solely on average test-set metrics.
Their approach highlights that:

Proper evaluation requires repeated training experiments
Coverage should be analyzed for each input location, not only on average.




Deeper Conceptual Contribution
A key insight of the paper is the separation between two types of uncertainty:
Model uncertainty (epistemic)
Uncertainty arising from limited training data and imperfect model estimation.
Data noise variance (aleatoric)
Intrinsic randomness in the data generation process.
Standard evaluation metrics combine these components into a single predictive uncertainty measure, making it impossible to determine whether either component is estimated correctly.



Ultimate Result
The authors show that models can achieve strong performance according to traditional metrics such as PICP or log-likelihood while still producing poorly calibrated uncertainty estimates locally.
Their proposed evaluation framework reveals these hidden weaknesses.

text:
3. Theoretical Framework & Technical Setup

Regression Formulation
The paper considers the standard regression setting:
[ Y X = x (f(x), ^2(x)) ]
Where:

(f(x)) is the true regression function
(^2(x)) is the noise variance

The goal of probabilistic regression models is therefore to estimate both:

the mean prediction ((x))
the predictive uncertainty around it.




Two Explicit Sources of Uncertainty
The paper distinguishes between two components:
Model uncertainty
Uncertainty due to imperfect estimation of the regression function. This uncertainty decreases with more training data.
Noise variance
Irreducible variability inherent in the data.
Many probabilistic models estimate both simultaneously, but existing evaluation metrics do not verify whether either estimate is correct.



Pointwise vs Marginal Coverage
This distinction is central to the paper.
Marginal coverage
Coverage averaged over the entire input distribution.
Example:
A 95% prediction interval should contain approximately 95% of the observations in the dataset.
Pointwise coverage
Coverage evaluated for each input location.
Example:
For a specific input (x), the interval should contain the true value 95% of the time across repeated training experiments.
The authors argue that pointwise coverage is the correct target, because marginal coverage can hide large local errors.

text:
4. Existing Evaluation Strategies Reviewed

PICP-Based Testing
For interval-based methods, the most common metric is:
Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP)
[ PICP = _{i=1}^{n} (y_i PI_i) ]
Where (PI_i) is the prediction interval for observation (i).
Coverage is usually reported alongside interval width metrics, because narrower intervals are preferred if coverage remains correct.



Log-Likelihood Evaluation
Methods that produce full predictive distributions are usually evaluated using test log-likelihood.
This benchmark methodology became popular following probabilistic backpropagation experiments on common regression datasets.
Typical benchmark datasets include:

Boston Housing
Energy Efficiency
Combined Cycle Power Plant
Protein Structure
Wine Quality
Year Prediction MSD

Performance is measured using:

average log-likelihood
RMSE

text:
5. Major Criticisms of Existing Evaluation

Criticism 1: Predictive Performance ≠ Correct Uncertainty
Even if a method produces good predictive distributions, it does not mean its uncertainty estimates are correct.
Errors in estimating model uncertainty may be compensated by incorrect estimates of noise variance.
Thus improved predictive metrics do not necessarily reflect improved uncertainty estimation.



Criticism 2: Single Test Sets Cannot Evaluate Coverage
Prediction intervals depend on:

the sampled training data
stochastic training procedures

Therefore interval evaluation must consider repeated experiments.
The authors show that even perfectly calibrated intervals may appear badly calibrated when evaluated on a single test split.



Criticism 3: PICP Only Measures Marginal Coverage
PICP measures average coverage across the dataset.
This means a model may have:

overly wide intervals in some regions
overly narrow intervals in others

yet still achieve the desired average coverage.
Such behavior is undesirable in practice.



Criticism 4: Log-Likelihood Conflates Mean Accuracy and Uncertainty
Log-likelihood evaluates the full predictive distribution.
However, improvements in log-likelihood may arise from:

better mean predictions
not necessarily better uncertainty estimates.

Therefore it is not a reliable metric for evaluating uncertainty quality.

href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#proposed-solution-simulation-based-testing
title: How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression
text:
6. Proposed Solution: Simulation-Based Testing

Main Idea
The authors propose evaluating uncertainty estimation methods through controlled simulation experiments.
Instead of relying on a single dataset split, the procedure repeatedly generates training data from a known data-generating process.
This allows the true regression function and variance to be known.



Evaluation Procedure

Define a data-generating distribution.
Generate a fixed test dataset.
Repeatedly sample training datasets.
Fit the uncertainty estimation method each time.
Compute coverage statistics across repetitions.




New Metrics Introduced
Prediction Interval Coverage Fraction (PICF)
Measures coverage probability for each input point across repeated experiments.
Confidence Interval Coverage Fraction (CICF)
Evaluates the correctness of confidence intervals for the estimated regression function.
Average Interval Width
Measures sharpness of intervals.
Brier Score
Used to quantify deviations between empirical coverage and the desired coverage level.
The Brier score also penalizes large variations in coverage across different inputs.

href: reviews/How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression.html#experimental-demonstrations
title: How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression
text:
7. Experimental Demonstrations

Methods Compared
The paper uses two uncertainty estimation approaches:

Naïve bootstrap
Concrete dropout

These methods were chosen because they are simple to implement and illustrate weaknesses of standard evaluation.



Homoscedastic Noise Simulation
The authors simulate the function:
[ f(x) = (2x - 1)^3 ]
with constant Gaussian noise.
Both bootstrap and dropout achieve correct PICP values.
However, analysis of pointwise coverage reveals large variations in interval quality across different input locations.



Heteroscedastic Noise Simulation
The noise variance is defined as:
[ (x) = 0.1 + x^2 ]
Bootstrap assumes constant noise while dropout can estimate heteroscedastic variance.
Although bootstrap achieves similar PICP values, pointwise evaluation shows significantly worse performance.
The Brier score correctly identifies dropout as the superior method.



Sparse Data Regions
The authors simulate bimodal input distributions to create regions with limited training data.
In these regions, uncertainty estimation becomes particularly important.
Conventional metrics such as PICP and log-likelihood incorrectly rank models, whereas pointwise coverage metrics reveal the true behavior.



Boston Housing Simulation
To demonstrate realism, the authors design simulations based on the Boston Housing dataset.
They:

Train a random forest to approximate the true regression function.
Train another model to estimate noise variance.
Simulate new response variables.

Both bootstrap and dropout appear acceptable under traditional metrics, yet detailed analysis reveals significant interval miscalibration.

title: How to Evaluate Uncertainty Estimates in Machine Learning for Regression
text:
8. Criticisms and Limitations

Limitation 1: Simulation Design Becomes Critical
The proposed evaluation framework depends on the quality of simulated data-generating processes.
If simulations do not reflect realistic conditions, evaluation results may not generalize.



Limitation 2: Dependence on Gaussian Noise Assumptions
Most experiments assume Gaussian noise distributions.
Real-world uncertainty distributions may be skewed or multi-modal.



Limitation 3: Limited Direct Applicability to Real Deployments
Simulation-based evaluation is ideal for research benchmarking.
However, it cannot be directly applied in real-world deployments where the true function is unknown.

This paper is highly relevant for research involving probabilistic forecasting models.
It provides strong methodological justification for several important arguments:

Aggregate calibration metrics may hide local failures.
Predictive likelihood improvements do not necessarily imply better uncertainty estimation.
Coverage evaluation should consider local behavior across the input space.

text:
11. One-Paragraph Literature Review Summary
Sluijterman, Cator, and Heskes analyze how uncertainty estimates are evaluated in regression machine learning and argue that the two dominant evaluation strategies, namely prediction interval coverage probability and test log-likelihood, are insufficient for assessing the correctness of uncertainty estimates. They demonstrate that models may appear well calibrated under traditional metrics while producing poorly calibrated intervals locally across the input space. The authors introduce a simulation-based evaluation framework that measures pointwise coverage using repeated training experiments, along with metrics such as prediction interval coverage fraction and Brier scores. Through experiments with bootstrap and dropout methods, they show that aggregate metrics can favor inferior models and fail to reveal important miscalibration behavior. Their work provides a methodological foundation for more rigorous evaluation of probabilistic regression models and highlights the importance of analyzing uncertainty behavior across the entire input domain.

title: Tier 2 Research Review: Theory & Justification
text:
Paper Title: Preventing dataset shift from breaking machine-learning biomarkers
Authors & Year: Jérôme Dockès, Gaël Varoquaux, Jean-Baptiste Poline (2021)
Venue (Journal/Conference): GigaScience (Oxford University Press) (Highly reputable, peer-reviewed open-access journal).
Link/DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/gigascience/giab055
Primary Topic/Concept: The mathematical breakdown of Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) under dataset shift, and why standard statistical “fixes” (like deconfounding) actually destroy predictive models.






The specific theory or mechanism explained:

The paper explains how dataset shift invalidates the core assumption of Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) in machine learning: that training data \(p_{source}(X,Y)\) and deployment data \(p_{target}(X,Y)\) come from the exact same distribution.

Their main argument/conclusion:

Cross-validation on a single dataset is fundamentally insufficient to guarantee real-world generalization if the dataset was subject to selection bias. Furthermore, attempting to “fix” this shift by regressing out correlated variables (deconfounding) actively harms predictive models; instead, one must use techniques like Importance Weighting or rely on sufficiently flexible/robust models.







Mathematical / Logical Foundation:

The ERM Failure: Machine learning models minimize empirical risk \(\hat{R}(f) = \frac{1}{n} \sum L(y_i, f(x_i))\). This is only a valid estimate of true risk if the training sample perfectly represents the target population.
Covariate vs. Prior Probability Shift: They mathematically separate Covariate Shift (where \(p(X)\) changes but \(p(Y|X)\) stays the same) from Prior Probability Shift (where \(p(Y)\) changes but \(p(X|Y)\) stays the same), noting that each requires different handling.

The “Fallacy of Deconfounding” (Crucial for Defense):

They prove (via simulated and real UKBiobank data) that tools from causal inference (like removing “confounders”) are disastrous for predictive modeling. Regressing out a shifting variable removes the predictive signal and drastically degrades accuracy.

Model Complexity Matters:

They demonstrate that highly flexible models (like Gradient Boosting or Non-linear SVMs) inherently handle covariate shifts better than over-constrained, simple linear models. In fact, applying “Importance Weighting” to a complex model can sometimes degrade performance by needlessly increasing the variance of the empirical risk.







What specific decision in my paper does this justify?

1. Justifying robust evaluation: I will use this paper to argue why standard cross-validation on historical PV data is insufficient, as historical weather/generation data inherently suffers from dataset shift (e.g., changing climate, sensor degradation).
2. Defending feature selection: I will use the “fallacy of deconfounding” argument as a theoretical shield against any reviewer who suggests I should have normalized or regressed out shifting meteorological variables (like temperature or seasonality) to make the data “stationary.” This paper proves that doing so destroys predictive signal.
3. Defending model complexity: I can use their findings to justify why deploying deep/flexible neural networks (rather than simple linear baselines) is actually a safeguard against certain types of covariate shift.

Where does this belong in my paper?

Introduction (Framing dataset shift as the primary reason historical ML models fail in real-world deployment).
Background / Related Work (Defining Covariate Shift vs. Prior Probability Shift).
Methodology (Defending my feature engineering choices and my choice not to strictly deconfound the input variables).







Assumptions made by the authors:

Importance Weighting \(\frac{p_{target}(x, y)}{p_{source}(x, y)}\) only works if there is strict distributional overlap (i.e., the support of the target distribution must be entirely included in the support of the source distribution). If a specific weather regime or failure state is completely missing from my training data, importance weighting cannot fix it.

When does this concept NOT apply?

This paper deals primarily with cross-sectional selection bias (e.g., demographic sampling in hospitals). While the math of covariate shift applies to energy, the paper does not explicitly address temporal concept drift (where the underlying physics \(p(Y|X)\) slowly changes over time, such as PV panel degradation).






Golden Quotes: - > “If the goal of the data analysis is purely predictive, no adjustment for confounding is necessary… applying procedures meant to adjust for confounding generally degrades prediction performance without solving the dataset shift issue.” (p. 2) - > “Often, flexible models can be more robust to dataset shifts, and thus generalize better, than linear models… an over-constrained (ill-specified) model may only fit well a restricted region of the feature space.” (p. 4) - > “Dataset shift does not call for simpler models because it is not a small-sample issue. Collecting more data from the same sources will not correct systematic dataset bias.” (p. 4)
Pre-written Justification Blurb: > “In predictive forecasting, addressing dataset shift through the removal of shifting covariates—often mistakenly referred to as ‘deconfounding’—is fundamentally flawed. As demonstrated by Dockès et al. (2021), while causal inference requires adjusting for confounders, doing so in a purely predictive setting strips the model of valuable signal and degrades generalization. Therefore, rather than regressing out non-stationary meteorological features, our methodology retains these variables, relying on the inherent capacity of highly flexible, non-linear neural architectures to generalize across covariate shifts without artificial data constraints.”

Collecting more data from the same sources will not correct systematic dataset bias.” (p. 4)
Pre-written Justification Blurb: > “In predictive forecasting, addressing dataset shift through the removal of shifting covariates—often mistakenly referred to as ‘deconfounding’—is fundamentally flawed. As demonstrated by Dockès et al. (2021), while causal inference requires adjusting for confounders, doing so in a purely predictive setting strips the model of valuable signal and degrades generalization. Therefore, rather than regressing out non-stationary meteorological features, our methodology retains these variables, relying on the inherent capacity of highly flexible, non-linear neural architectures to generalize across covariate shifts without artificial data constraints.”

2. Core Contributions, Novelty & Motivation

Motivation: Why Uncertainty Validation Matters
Many modern machine learning models provide uncertainty estimates alongside predictions. These may come from:

Bayesian neural networks

Gaussian processes

ensemble models

quantile regression

probabilistic boosting methods

However, simply producing uncertainty estimates does not guarantee they are reliable. A model might output uncertainty values that appear reasonable but do not correspond to the actual prediction errors.
The paper argues that existing validation approaches mostly test average calibration, which checks whether uncertainties are correct on average. However, average correctness does not guarantee local reliability.
For safety-critical applications such as energy forecasting, autonomous systems, or scientific modelling, uncertainty estimates must be reliable for individual predictions and across the input space, not just globally.



Main Conceptual Contribution
The paper introduces a three-component framework for validating uncertainty quantification:

Average Calibration
Consistency
Adaptivity

These three concepts together provide a much more complete validation framework for probabilistic models.



Average Calibration
Average calibration tests whether the predicted uncertainty magnitude matches the overall error dispersion.
For variance-based uncertainty models, this typically means:
[ Var(E) u_E^2 ]
Where:

(E) = prediction error

(u_E) = predicted uncertainty

If a model is well calibrated, then the variance of the errors should match the average predicted uncertainty variance.
However, this check alone is insufficient because overestimation in some regions and underestimation in others can cancel out.



Consistency
Consistency tests whether uncertainties remain correct across different levels of predicted uncertainty.
In other words:

If the model says uncertainty is high, do we actually observe larger errors?

Mathematically this is expressed through conditional calibration:

Where

This ensures that uncertainty estimates are correctly scaled across different uncertainty magnitudes.



Adaptivity
Adaptivity is the paper’s most important conceptual contribution.
Adaptivity tests whether uncertainties remain reliable across the input space.
Instead of conditioning on predicted uncertainty, the analysis conditions on input features:
[ Var(Z X = x) ]
This evaluates whether uncertainty estimates remain valid in different regions of the data distribution.
Example:
A solar power forecasting model might produce correct uncertainty on average but fail during:

cloudy conditions

winter months

high irradiance periods

Adaptivity analysis would reveal these failures.

4. Validation Strategy
The paper validates its framework using two approaches:

Synthetic Case Studies
Six synthetic datasets are constructed to represent different failure modes.
These include cases where models are:

fully calibrated and adaptive

calibrated but inconsistent

calibrated but not adaptive

completely miscalibrated

This allows the author to demonstrate how different diagnostic tools respond to known ground truth.



Reanalysis of Existing ML Studies
The framework is also applied to previously published uncertainty quantification studies.
This reanalysis shows that many published models that appear well-calibrated actually exhibit:

local miscalibration
inconsistent uncertainty scaling
lack of adaptivity across feature space

Thus the standard validation methods used in prior literature may overestimate model reliability.

5. Diagnostic Tools Evaluated
The paper evaluates several common UQ validation tools.

Calibration Curves
Calibration curves compare predicted uncertainty with observed error.
These are useful but mainly test average calibration.



Reliability Diagrams
Reliability diagrams evaluate calibration across different uncertainty bins.
They test consistency, but are sensitive to:

bin size

sample size

data distribution




Confidence Curves
Confidence curves measure model error as predictions are filtered by uncertainty ranking.
However, the paper argues that oracle-based confidence curves are misleading, because they do not test calibration directly.
Instead, the paper proposes probabilistic reference curves.



Local Z-Variance Diagnostics
The paper proposes analysing local variance of standardized errors.
This allows detection of:

local over-confidence
local under-confidence




Local Coverage Probability
For interval predictions, local coverage probability evaluates whether predicted intervals remain valid across:

uncertainty levels
input features

6. Key Findings

Average Calibration is Insufficient
A model can appear perfectly calibrated globally while being locally unreliable.



Adaptivity is Often Ignored
Most prior work evaluates calibration and consistency but does not evaluate adaptivity.
This means uncertainty models may fail under certain conditions without detection.



Many Standard Metrics Are Weak
Common scalar metrics such as:

ENCE

AUCO

do not guarantee consistency or adaptivity.
They should not be used as the sole evidence of reliable uncertainty.



Reliability Diagrams Depend on Binning
Improper binning can hide important uncertainty failures.
Careful bin selection is necessary.

7. Limitations of the Study

Framework Requires Expert Interpretation
The methodology relies heavily on diagnostic plots rather than automated metrics.
Practitioners must interpret results carefully.



Feature Selection for Adaptivity is Non-Trivial
Choosing the right feature dimension to analyse adaptivity requires domain knowledge.
In high-dimensional models this can be difficult.



Focus on Diagnosis Rather Than Correction
The paper provides tools for identifying problems but does not propose new algorithms to fix them.

10. Bottom Line
The paper provides a conceptual framework for validating uncertainty quantification that goes beyond standard calibration tests.
It argues that reliable uncertainty estimates must satisfy three properties:

Calibration — correct on average

Consistency — correct across uncertainty levels

Adaptivity — correct across the input space

Many existing studies only validate the first property.
Therefore, rigorous uncertainty validation must evaluate all three dimensions to ensure that uncertainty estimates remain trustworthy in real-world applications.
